metadata.title: How to Measure the Quality of an AI Product

beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. An AI product can be fast, fluent, and still bad. Quality has many dimensions, and each one needs its own measure. Here is the toolkit a product manager should know.

props.segment: How to Measure the Quality of an AI Product
props.command: How do I measure the quality of an AI product?

beats.narration_text: AI quality is a set of measures, and no single number is enough. A product can score well on one and fail users on another, so you choose measures by what failing would cost.

props.text:
AI quality is
one accuracy score
that you track.
props.triggerWords: one accuracy score, that you track
props.replacementWords: a set of measures, and no single number is enough

beats.narration_text: Here are nine measures. Groundedness. Relevance. Accuracy. Hallucination rate. Precision. Recall. Response quality. Latency. And user satisfaction. No product needs all nine equally, so a product manager chooses by what failing would cost.

props.caption: Choose by the cost of failing

beats.narration_text: Start with the answer itself. Accuracy asks: is it correct? Relevance asks: does it answer what was actually asked? Groundedness asks: is it supported by the sources it was given? And hallucination rate counts how often the product states something unsupported.

layers.title: Relevance
layers.sub: Does it answer what was asked?

layers.title: Groundedness
layers.sub: Is it supported by the sources given?

layers.title: Hallucination rate
layers.sub: How often it states unsupported claims

beats.narration_text: To measure any of this, build a test set: real questions, the answers you expect, and the sources that support them. Run every release against the same set and score each measure. Now you can compare this release to the last one, instead of arguing about how it feels.

Precision and recall come from search. Precision asks: of the passages retrieved, how many were useful? Recall asks: of all the useful passages, how many were found? They trade off. Retrieve more and recall rises, but precision falls. Which matters more depends on what a miss costs versus what noise costs.

layers.title: Precision
layers.sub: Of what it found, how much was useful?

layers.title: Recall
layers.sub: Of what was useful, how much did it find?

layers.title: The trade-off
layers.sub: Raising one often lowers the other

beats.narration_text: Some quality is felt, not computed. Human reviewers can rate responses against a rubric. A second model can act as a judge, which scales but must be checked against humans. Latency matters, because slow answers feel wrong. Cost per answer decides if you can afford it. And user signals tell you what people truly value.

Finally, how measures mislead. Averages hide the worst failures, so read the bad cases. Metrics can be gamed, so refresh the test set. A model judge can be biased, so spot-check it with humans. And a good score is not a good product, so always check real outcomes.
So, measuring quality. No single number is enough. Check accuracy, relevance, groundedness and hallucinations. Test on a fixed set. Add speed, cost and users. And read the worst cases.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I am a product manager for an AI feature that does this: [describe it]. Pick the five quality measures that matter most for it, explain each in one plain sentence, write a ten-question test set with expected answers, and suggest a pass threshold for launch. Then tell me which measure could look good while users are still unhappy. The last sentence is the sharpest. A measure that looks good while users are unhappy is a measure you are over-trusting, so check that one against real user outcomes first. Pause here and run it on your own product.
